l: rich man (the man who asked about eternal life), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 10
s: The man runs to Jesus, kneels, and asks what to do to inherit eternal life, saying he has kept the commandments from his youth. Jesus, looking at him with love, tells him to sell what he has, give to the poor, and follow him, but the man goes away sorrowful because he has great possessions.

l: riches, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 10
s: Jesus says it is difficult for those who have riches, and hard for those who trust in them, to enter God's Kingdom, comparing it to a camel going through a needle's eye. The disciples are astonished, and Jesus answers that with God all things are possible.

l: Jesus's death and resurrection (predicted), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 10
s: On the way up to Jerusalem Jesus tells the twelve that the Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, condemned to death, and handed to the Gentiles. They will mock, spit on, scourge, and kill him, and on the third day he will rise again.

l: James, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 10
s: James, with his brother John, sons of Zebedee, asks Jesus to grant that they sit at his right and left in his glory. Jesus says they will drink his cup and share his baptism, but that those seats are for those for whom they have been prepared.

l: John, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 10
s: John, with James, sons of Zebedee, asks Jesus for the seats at his right and left in his glory, and says they are able to drink his cup. Jesus says the seats are not his to give, and the other ten become indignant at the two.

l: Bartimaeus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 10
s: Bartimaeus, the blind son of Timaeus, sits begging by the road at Jericho and cries out to Jesus, son of David, for mercy despite being rebuked by many. Jesus calls him and says his faith has made him well, and he receives his sight and follows Jesus on the way.

l: The Good News According to Mark, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: Near Jerusalem, Jesus sends two disciples to fetch a young donkey, rides it into the city while crowds spread garments and branches and cry out "Hosanna," and enters the temple before going out to Bethany with the twelve. The next day he curses a leafy fig tree that has no fruit, then returns to the temple, throws out buyers and sellers, overturns the money changers' tables, and declares it was meant to be a house of prayer but has become a den of robbers. The chief priests and scribes seek to destroy him, fearing the astonished multitude. The next morning the disciples find the fig tree withered, and Jesus teaches about faith, prayer, and forgiveness. Back in the temple, the chief priests, scribes, and elders challenge his authority, and he counters by asking whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men; they refuse to answer, so he refuses to tell them his authority.

l: Jesus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: Jesus sends disciples for a donkey, rides into Jerusalem to cries of "Hosanna," and enters the temple. He curses a fruitless fig tree, drives out sellers and buyers in the temple, teaches on faith, prayer, and forgiveness, and silences the religious leaders' challenge with a question about John's baptism.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: Two disciples fetch the young donkey as Jesus instructed and answer those who question them with his words. The disciples hear Jesus curse the fig tree, and Peter later remarks on its withering, prompting Jesus' teaching on faith.

l: Jerusalem, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: Jesus approaches and enters Jerusalem, where crowds welcome him, and he repeatedly goes into the temple there, returning to Bethany in the evenings. The chief priests, scribes, and elders in the city plan to destroy him and question his authority.

l: young donkey (Jesus's mount), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: A young donkey, tied outside in the street and never before sat on, is untied by two disciples after they say the Lord needs it. Garments are thrown on it and Jesus rides it toward Jerusalem.

l: temple, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: Jesus enters the temple, looks around, and leaves in the evening; the next day he drives out sellers and buyers and forbids carrying containers through it. He says it is to be a house of prayer for all nations but has been made a den of robbers, and later the leaders confront him there about his authority.

l: crowd (people who welcomed Jesus), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: Many in the crowd spread their garments and cut branches to spread on the road, and those in front and behind cry out "Hosanna" and bless the coming kingdom of David. The whole multitude is also described as astonished at Jesus' teaching, and the people are feared by the leaders.

l: fig tree, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: Jesus, hungry, finds only leaves on a fig tree, as it was not the season for figs, and tells it that no one will eat its fruit again. The next morning the disciples see it withered from the roots, and Peter points this out.

l: money changers and sellers in the temple, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: Jesus throws out those selling and buying in the temple and overturns the money changers' tables and the seats of the dove sellers. He accuses them of making the house of prayer a den of robbers.

l: chief priests, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: The chief priests hear Jesus' words in the temple and seek a way to destroy him, fearing him because of the crowd's astonishment. Later, with scribes and elders, they ask by what authority he acts, and they will not answer his question about John's baptism for fear of the people.

l: scribes, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: The scribes hear Jesus' teaching in the temple and, with the chief priests, look for a way to destroy him. They join the chief priests and elders in challenging his authority and, unable to answer his question about John, say "We don't know."

l: triumphal entry, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: Jesus rides a borrowed young donkey toward Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives area, with garments and branches spread on the road. Crowds in front and behind cry "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," and bless the coming kingdom of David.

l: cleansing of the temple, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: Jesus enters the temple, throws out sellers and buyers, overturns the money changers' tables and dove sellers' seats, and bars carrying containers through it. He cites that it should be a house of prayer for all nations, and the chief priests and scribes respond by seeking to destroy him.

l: faith and prayer, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: Prompted by the withered fig tree, Jesus tells the disciples to have faith in God, saying whoever without doubt tells a mountain to be cast into the sea will have it. He says whatever is prayed for in belief will be received, and that praying people must forgive others so the Father will forgive them.

l: John, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: John's baptism becomes the subject of Jesus' counter-question to the leaders, asking whether it was from heaven or from men. The leaders will not answer because they fear either response, noting that all the people held John to really be a prophet.

l: authority of Jesus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 11
s: The chief priests, scribes, and elders ask by what authority Jesus does these things and who gave it to him. Jesus answers with a question about John's baptism, and when they say they don't know, he declines to tell them his authority.

l: The Good News According to Mark, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Jesus tells a parable of a man who planted a vineyard and rented it to farmers who beat and killed his servants and finally killed his beloved son; Jesus says the lord of the vineyard will destroy them and give the vineyard to others, and quotes Scripture about the rejected stone. The leaders perceive the parable is against them and, after sending Pharisees and Herodians to trap him over paying taxes to Caesar, Jesus answers 'Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.' The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a question about a woman who married seven brothers, and Jesus answers that they err in not knowing the Scriptures or God's power. A scribe asks which commandment is greatest, and Jesus names loving the Lord God and loving one's neighbor, telling the scribe he is not far from God's Kingdom. Jesus then questions how the Christ can be David's son, warns against the scribes, and praises a poor widow who gave two small coins into the treasury as giving more than the rich.

l: Jesus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Jesus speaks in parables, quotes Scripture about the rejected stone, and answers questions about taxes to Caesar, the resurrection, and the greatest commandment. He tells a scribe he is not far from God's Kingdom, asks how the Christ can be David's son, warns against the scribes, and commends the poor widow's gift.

l: man who planted a vineyard (parable), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: The man planted a vineyard, put a hedge around it, dug a pit for the wine press, built a tower, rented it to farmers, and went to another country. He sent servants and finally his beloved son; Jesus says he will come, destroy the farmers, and give the vineyard to others.

l: vineyard (parable), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: The vineyard was planted with a hedge, a wine press pit, and a tower, and rented to farmers. The farmers cast the son out of it, and Jesus says it will be given to others.

l: farmers (parable), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: The farmers beat one servant, stoned and wounded another, and killed another along with many others. They then killed the heir, casting him out of the vineyard, and Jesus says the lord will destroy them.

l: beloved son (parable), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: The man sends his beloved son last, saying they will respect him. The farmers recognize him as heir, kill him, and cast him out of the vineyard.

l: Parable of the vineyard, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Jesus tells this parable about a man, his vineyard, rebellious farmers, and his murdered son, ending with the lord destroying the farmers and giving the vineyard to others. The leaders perceive it was spoken against them and try to seize him but fear the multitude.

l: Pharisees, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Some of the Pharisees are sent, with the Herodians, to trap Jesus with words. They ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, and Jesus, knowing their hypocrisy, answers them and they marvel.

l: Herodians, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Some Herodians are sent with Pharisees to trap Jesus with words about paying taxes to Caesar. They marvel greatly at his answer.

l: Caesar, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Caesar's image and inscription are on the denarius that Jesus asks to see. Jesus says to give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's.

l: taxes to Caesar, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: The Pharisees and Herodians ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. Jesus has a denarius brought, notes it bears Caesar's image, and says to give Caesar what is Caesar's and God what is God's.

l: Sadducees, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: The Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, ask Jesus about a woman who married seven brothers in turn. Jesus tells them they are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God, and are badly mistaken.

l: resurrection, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: The Sadducees deny the resurrection and challenge Jesus about it. Jesus says that when people rise they neither marry nor are given in marriage but are like angels in heaven, and that God is God of the living, not the dead.

l: seven brothers and the woman, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: In the Sadducees' scenario, seven brothers each take the same woman as wife and die without children, and the woman dies last. The Sadducees ask whose wife she will be in the resurrection.

l: God, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Jesus says God spoke to Moses at the Bush, 'I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,' and is God of the living, not the dead. He is the Lord who is one, to be loved with all the heart, soul, mind, and strength, and the scribe says this love is more important than burnt offerings and sacrifices.

l: scribe (who asked about the greatest commandment), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: This scribe heard the questioning, saw that Jesus answered well, and asked which commandment is greatest. He affirms Jesus' answer, saying love is more than offerings and sacrifices, and Jesus tells him he is not far from God's Kingdom.

l: scribes, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Jesus asks how the scribes can say the Christ is David's son, and warns against them for liking long robes, greetings, best seats, and long pretentious prayers. He says they devour widows' houses and will receive greater condemnation.

l: greatest commandments, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Jesus names the first as hearing that the Lord is one and loving God with all heart, soul, mind, and strength. The second is to love one's neighbor as oneself, and no other commandment is greater.

l: Christ, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Jesus asks how the scribes can say the Christ is the son of David when David himself, in the Holy Spirit, calls him Lord. He cites the saying 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.'

l: David, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Jesus says David, speaking in the Holy Spirit, said 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.' Because David calls the Christ Lord, Jesus asks how he can be David's son.

l: treasury, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: Jesus sits opposite the treasury and watches the multitude cast in money, with many rich people giving much. He observes that a poor widow's two small coins amounted to more than all the others gave.

l: poor widow, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 12
s: A poor widow casts two small brass coins, equal to a quadrans, into the treasury. Jesus tells his disciples she gave more than all the others because she gave all she had to live on out of her poverty.

l: The Good News According to Mark, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 13
s: As Jesus leaves the temple, a disciple admires its stones and buildings, and Jesus predicts that not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives, Peter, James, John, and Andrew privately ask when this will happen and what the sign will be. Jesus warns them about deceivers, wars, earthquakes, famines, persecution before councils and rulers, family betrayal, and hatred for his name, while the Good News is preached to all nations. He describes the abomination of desolation, a time of unparalleled oppression that is shortened for the chosen ones, and false christs and prophets, followed by cosmic signs and the coming of the Son of Man, who gathers the chosen ones. He teaches the fig tree parable, says no one but the Father knows the day or hour, and closes with the parable of a traveling man, urging everyone to watch.

l: Jesus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 13
s: Jesus predicts the total destruction of the temple's buildings and, on the Mount of Olives, answers Peter, James, John, and Andrew privately about the signs ahead. He warns against deception, foretells persecution, the abomination of desolation, great oppression, and the coming of the Son of Man, and declares that his words will not pass away. He says that of that day or hour no one knows, not even the Son, but only the Father.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 13
s: One disciple admires the temple's stones and buildings, and Peter, James, John, and Andrew privately ask Jesus when these things will happen and what the sign will be. They are warned of deception, of being delivered to councils, beaten in synagogues, and hated by all, and told to rely on the Holy Spirit's words and to endure to the end. They are told to watch, keep alert, and pray.

l: temple, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 13
s: The temple is the place Jesus leaves as a disciple remarks on its great stones and buildings. Jesus says that not one stone will be left on another that will not be thrown down.

l: abomination of desolation, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 13
s: Jesus says it was spoken of by Daniel the prophet and will be seen standing where it ought not, with the reader told to understand. When it is seen, those in Judea must flee to the mountains without taking anything from house or field.

l: great oppression (tribulation of those days), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 13
s: Jesus describes it as oppression unlike any from the beginning of creation until now, and never to be again. He says the days were shortened by the Lord for the sake of the chosen ones, since otherwise no flesh would be saved. He tells them to pray the flight won't be in winter, and says woe comes to those with child or nursing babies.

l: false christs and false prophets, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 13
s: Jesus says they will arise and show signs and wonders to lead astray, if possible, even the chosen ones. He instructs the disciples not to believe anyone who says 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'Look, there!'. Earlier, many who come in his name saying 'I am he!' are also said to lead many astray.

l: chosen ones, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 13
s: The chosen ones are the reason the days of oppression are shortened, and false christs and prophets try to lead them astray if possible. At the coming of the Son of Man, his angels gather them from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of the sky.

l: coming of the Son of Man, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 13
s: After the oppression, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give light, stars will fall, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken. Then people will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory, and he will send out his angels to gather the chosen ones. Its day and hour are known only to the Father.

l: man traveling (parable), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 13
s: In the parable, a man goes to another country, leaving his house, giving authority and work to each servant, and commanding the doorkeeper to keep watch. The lord of the house's return time is unknown, whether evening, midnight, rooster crow, or morning, and he must not find them sleeping when he comes suddenly.

l: watchfulness, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 13
s: Jesus repeatedly commands watchfulness: be careful of being led astray, watch, keep alert, and pray, because no one knows when the time is. He closes by saying that what he tells the disciples he tells all: Watch!

l: The Good News According to Mark, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: Two days before the Passover, the chief priests and scribes plot to seize and kill Jesus, while a woman anoints him at Bethany and Judas Iscariot goes to the chief priests to betray him. Jesus eats the Passover meal with the twelve, predicts that one of them will betray him and that all will stumble, and gives them the bread and the cup as his body and blood of the new covenant. At Gethsemane he prays in distress while Peter, James, and John fall asleep, and Judas arrives with an armed crowd and identifies Jesus with a kiss, after which the disciples flee. Jesus is taken to the high priest, where false testimony fails to agree, and he answers that he is the Christ and is condemned for blasphemy. Meanwhile Peter, as Jesus predicted, denies him three times before the rooster crows a second time, and weeps.

l: Jesus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: Jesus defends the woman who anoints him, saying she has anointed his body beforehand for burial. He predicts his betrayal, Peter's denial, and the disciples' scattering, prays in anguish at Gethsemane, is arrested, and answers the high priest that he is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed. He is condemned as worthy of death and is spat on and beaten.

l: chief priests, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: The chief priests and scribes seek to seize Jesus by deception and kill him, but not during the feast. They are glad when Judas offers to deliver him and promise him money, then send a multitude to arrest him and gather with the elders and scribes to seek testimony against him.

l: woman (who anointed Jesus), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: At Simon the leper's house in Bethany, the woman breaks an alabaster jar of costly pure nard ointment and pours it over Jesus' head. Some grumble that it was wasted, but Jesus says she did a good work and that what she did will be spoken of as a memorial to her wherever the Good News is preached.

l: Judas Iscariot, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: Judas, one of the twelve, goes to the chief priests to deliver Jesus to them, and they promise him money. He later arrives at Gethsemane with the crowd, gives the sign of a kiss, and greets Jesus as "Rabbi! Rabbi!" to identify him for arrest.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: The twelve eat the Passover with Jesus, and each asks "Surely not I?" when he says one of them will betray him. Jesus says it is one of the twelve who dips with him in the dish. They all vow not to deny him, but they all leave him and flee when he is arrested.

l: Last Supper meal (bread and cup), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: During the Passover meal Jesus blesses and breaks bread, giving it to the disciples and saying, "This is my body." He gives thanks over the cup, which they all drink, saying it is his blood of the new covenant poured out for many, and says he will not drink the fruit of the vine again until he drinks it anew in God's Kingdom.

l: Peter, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: Peter insists he will not be offended even if all others are and says he will not deny Jesus even if he must die with him. He is one of three taken deeper into Gethsemane, falls asleep, and later follows the arrested Jesus into the high priest's courtyard, where he denies him three times and weeps when he remembers Jesus' words.

l: Gethsemane, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: Gethsemane is the place where Jesus brings his disciples after the meal and takes Peter, James, and John further with him. There he prays, "Abba, Father," asking that the cup be removed yet submitting to the Father's will, finds the disciples sleeping three times, and is arrested.

l: crowd that arrested Jesus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: A multitude with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests, scribes, and elders, comes with Judas and seizes Jesus after the kiss. Jesus asks why they come against him as against a robber when he taught daily in the temple, and says this happens so the Scriptures might be fulfilled.

l: high priest, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: The high priest receives Jesus after his arrest, asks why he does not answer the testimony against him, and asks if he is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed. When Jesus says "I am," he tears his clothes, declares it blasphemy, and the council condemns Jesus as worthy of death. One of his maids is the first to challenge Peter.

l: Peter's denial, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: In the high priest's courtyard, Peter is identified as being with Jesus by a maid, again by the maid, and then by bystanders who note his Galilean speech. He denies it each time, the third time cursing and swearing he does not know the man, and the rooster crows a second time, fulfilling Jesus' prediction.

l: betrayal of Jesus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 14
s: Jesus foretells that one of the twelve who eats with him will betray him, and says woe to that man. Judas carries it out by arranging with the chief priests, leading an armed crowd to Gethsemane, and identifying Jesus with a kiss, which leads to Jesus' arrest.

l: The Good News According to Mark, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 15
s: In the morning the chief priests, elders, scribes and council bind Jesus and deliver him to Pilate, who questions him about being King of the Jews while Jesus gives little answer. Pilate, perceiving the priests' envy but wishing to please the crowd, releases the insurgent Barabbas and hands Jesus over to be flogged and crucified. The soldiers mock Jesus with a purple cloak and crown of thorns, then lead him out, compelling Simon of Cyrene to carry his cross to Golgotha. Jesus is crucified between two robbers, mocked by passersby, priests and the robbers, and after darkness falls he cries out and dies, the temple veil tears, and the centurion declares him the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathaea asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen and lays it in a rock-cut tomb, while Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses watch.

l: Jesus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 15
s: Jesus is bound, handed to Pilate, and answers the question of whether he is King of the Jews with "So you say," then makes no further answer. He is flogged, mocked by the soldiers, crucified at the third hour, and cries "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" before giving up the spirit. His body is taken down, wrapped in linen and laid in a tomb.

l: Pilate, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 15
s: Pilate questions Jesus, marvels at his silence, and perceives that the chief priests delivered him up out of envy. Wishing to please the multitude, he releases Barabbas and hands Jesus over to be flogged and crucified. Later he is surprised that Jesus is already dead, confirms it with the centurion, and grants the body to Joseph.

l: chief priests, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 15
s: The chief priests, with the elders, scribes and council, bind Jesus and deliver him to Pilate, accusing him of many things. They stir up the multitude to ask for Barabbas instead. At the cross they mock Jesus, saying he saved others but cannot save himself.

l: multitude, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 15
s: The multitude asks Pilate to do as he always does and release a prisoner. Stirred up by the chief priests, they ask for Barabbas and cry out repeatedly "Crucify him!" even when Pilate asks what evil Jesus has done.

l: Barabbas, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 15
s: Barabbas is a prisoner bound with fellow insurgents who had committed murder in the insurrection. He is released by Pilate in place of Jesus at the multitude's request.

l: soldiers, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 15
s: The soldiers lead Jesus into the Praetorium and call together the whole cohort. They clothe him in purple, crown him with thorns, salute him as King of the Jews, strike him with a reed, spit on him and bow in mockery. They then lead him out to crucify him, compel Simon of Cyrene to carry the cross, and divide his garments by casting lots.

l: cross, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 15
s: The cross is carried to Golgotha by Simon of Cyrene, whom the soldiers compel to do so. Passersby and the chief priests taunt Jesus to come down from it.

l: crucifixion of Jesus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 15
s: Jesus is crucified at Golgotha at the third hour, with an inscription reading "THE KING OF THE JEWS" and two robbers crucified on either side. He is mocked by passersby, priests and the robbers; darkness covers the land from the sixth to the ninth hour, and he dies with a loud cry. The temple veil is torn in two and the centurion declares him the Son of God.

l: Joseph of Arimathaea, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 15
s: Joseph of Arimathaea, a prominent council member looking for God's Kingdom, boldly asks Pilate for Jesus' body on the Preparation Day. He buys linen, takes Jesus down, wraps him, lays him in a rock-cut tomb and rolls a stone against the door.

l: tomb (Jesus' tomb), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 15
s: The tomb is cut out of rock, and Jesus' body, wrapped in linen, is laid in it by Joseph of Arimathaea. A stone is rolled against its door, and Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses see where he was laid.

l: The Good News According to Mark, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 16
s: After the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bring spices to anoint Jesus and find the stone rolled away from the tomb. A young man in a white robe tells them Jesus has risen and instructs them to tell his disciples and Peter that he goes before them into Galilee. The women flee in fear and say nothing to anyone. Jesus appears first to Mary Magdalene, then to two others on a walk, and finally to the eleven, whom he rebukes for unbelief before commissioning them to preach the Good News to all creation and describing signs that will accompany believers. Jesus is received up into heaven and sits at God's right hand, and the disciples go out and preach everywhere.

l: Jesus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 16
s: Jesus is announced as risen from the tomb and appears first to Mary Magdalene, then in another form to two on a walk, then to the eleven, whom he rebukes for unbelief. He commissions them to preach the Good News to all creation, then is received up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God.

l: Mary Magdalene, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 16
s: Mary Magdalene goes with the other women to the tomb with spices, hears the young man's announcement, and flees in fear. Jesus appears to her first, having cast seven demons out of her, and she tells his mourning followers, who disbelieve her.

l: Mary the mother of James, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 16
s: Mary the mother of James buys spices with the other women and goes to the tomb. She sees the young man, hears that Jesus has risen, and flees in trembling, telling no one.

l: Salome, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 16
s: Salome buys spices with the two Marys and goes to the tomb to anoint Jesus. She is amazed by the young man's message, then flees afraid and says nothing.

l: young man in linen cloth, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 16
s: A young man in a white robe sits on the right side inside the tomb. He tells the women not to be amazed, announces that Jesus has risen, shows them the place where he lay, and tells them to tell his disciples and Peter that Jesus goes before them into Galilee.

l: tomb (Jesus' tomb), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 16
s: The women find the very large stone at the tomb already rolled back. Inside, they see the young man and learn that Jesus is not there but has risen.

l: disciples (of Jesus), The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 16
s: The disciples mourn and weep, and disbelieve Mary Magdalene's report and later that of the two who saw Jesus on a walk. Jesus appears to the eleven at the table and rebukes their unbelief and hardness of heart, then sends them to preach. They go out and preach everywhere, with the Lord working with them and confirming the word by signs.

l: resurrection of Jesus, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 16
s: The young man declares that Jesus, the crucified Nazarene, has risen and is not in the tomb. Jesus is then seen by Mary Magdalene, two others, and the eleven, though many who hear of it at first do not believe.

l: Good News, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 16
s: Jesus commands the eleven to preach the Good News to the whole creation, saying that those who believe and are baptized will be saved and those who disbelieve will be condemned. The disciples go out and preach it everywhere.

l: believers, The Good News According to Mark, Chapter 16
s: Jesus says believers will be saved if baptized, and that signs will accompany them: casting out demons in his name, speaking with new languages, taking up serpents, being unharmed by deadly drink, and healing the sick by laying on hands.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 1
s: The chapter opens with a preface addressed to Theophilus, then tells of Zacharias, a priest, and his barren wife Elizabeth, who are told by the angel Gabriel in the temple that they will have a son named John. Because Zacharias doubts, he is made mute until the child's birth. Gabriel is then sent to Mary, a virgin in Nazareth pledged to Joseph, announcing she will conceive Jesus, the Son of the Most High, by the Holy Spirit. Mary visits Elizabeth, who blesses her, and Mary speaks a song of praise to God. John is born, Zacharias writes his name and regains speech, and he prophesies about God's salvation and John's role before the Lord.

l: Zacharias, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 1
s: Zacharias, a priest of the division of Abijah, is told by Gabriel in the temple that Elizabeth will bear a son named John; he asks how he can be sure and is struck mute for not believing. He regains speech after writing 'His name is John' and then prophesies, blessing God for redemption and describing John as a prophet who will prepare the Lord's ways.

l: Elizabeth, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 1
s: Elizabeth, a daughter of Aaron and wife of Zacharias, was barren and old but conceived, hiding herself five months and saying the Lord had taken away her reproach. She blesses Mary when she visits, is filled with the Holy Spirit, gives birth to a son, and insists he be called John.

l: John, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 1
s: John is foretold by Gabriel as one who will be great before the Lord, drink no wine, be filled with the Holy Spirit from the womb, and go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. He leaps in Elizabeth's womb at Mary's greeting, is born and named John on the eighth day, and grows strong in spirit, living in the desert until his public appearance to Israel.

l: Gabriel, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 1
s: Gabriel identifies himself as one who stands in the presence of God. He announces John's birth to Zacharias and makes him mute for his unbelief, then in the sixth month is sent to Mary in Nazareth to announce that she will conceive Jesus.

l: Mary, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 1
s: Mary, a virgin of Nazareth pledged to Joseph of David's house, is told by Gabriel she has found favor with God and will bear Jesus. She accepts, saying 'let it be done to me according to your word,' visits Elizabeth, is called blessed and the mother of Elizabeth's Lord, and sings praise to God before staying about three months and returning home.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 1
s: Jesus is the son Gabriel says Mary will conceive and name. He is to be great, called the Son of the Most High and Son of God, given the throne of his father David, and reign over the house of Jacob forever in a Kingdom without end.

l: God, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 1
s: God sends Gabriel to Zacharias and to Mary, hears Zacharias's request, and takes away Elizabeth's reproach. Mary and Zacharias praise him as Savior and as the one who has visited and redeemed his people, shown mercy, and remembered his covenant with Abraham.

l: birth of John, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 1
s: John's birth is foretold by Gabriel to Zacharias, and Elizabeth conceives afterward. When he is born, neighbors and relatives rejoice at the Lord's mercy, and on the eighth day Elizabeth and Zacharias both insist on the name John, which frees Zacharias's tongue and causes fear and talk throughout the hill country of Judea.

l: Gabriel's announcement of Jesus' conception, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 1
s: In the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy, Gabriel tells Mary in Nazareth that she will conceive and bear a son named Jesus. When she asks how, he says the Holy Spirit will come on her and the power of the Most High will overshadow her, notes Elizabeth's pregnancy as a sign, and says nothing spoken by God is impossible.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 tells how, under a decree from Caesar Augustus, Joseph and the pregnant Mary travel from Nazareth to Bethlehem, where Mary gives birth to her firstborn son and lays him in a feeding trough. An angel of the Lord announces the birth to shepherds, a multitude of the heavenly army praises God, and the shepherds visit the child and spread the news. After the circumcision and naming of Jesus, his parents present him at the temple in Jerusalem, where Simeon and the prophetess Anna recognize him and Simeon speaks to Mary of a sword piercing her soul. The family returns to Nazareth, and at twelve Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem, where his parents find him after three days among the teachers in the temple and he speaks of being in his Father's house. He returns with them to Nazareth, is subject to them, and increases in wisdom, stature, and favor with God and men.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: Jesus is born in Bethlehem, wrapped in cloth and laid in a feeding trough, and is named Jesus on the eighth day as the angel had given before his conception. He is presented at the temple, recognized by Simeon and Anna, and grows strong in spirit and wisdom. At twelve he stays behind in Jerusalem, amazes the teachers in the temple, says he must be in his Father's house, then returns to Nazareth and is subject to his parents while increasing in wisdom, stature, and favor with God and men.

l: Mary, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: Mary, pledged to Joseph and pregnant, goes with him to Bethlehem to enroll and gives birth to her firstborn son there. She keeps the shepherds' sayings, pondering them in her heart, and Simeon tells her a sword will pierce through her own soul. When Jesus is twelve she and Joseph search for him for three days, she questions him in the temple, and she keeps all these sayings in her heart.

l: Joseph, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: Joseph goes up from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem, the city of David, because he is of David's house and family, to enroll with Mary. He is present at the shepherds' visit, the presentation at the temple, and the return to Nazareth. He and Mary lose Jesus in Jerusalem at the Passover when Jesus is twelve and find him in the temple after three days.

l: Nazareth, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: Nazareth in Galilee is the city Joseph leaves to go to Bethlehem for the enrollment. After fulfilling the law's requirements in Jerusalem, the family returns there as their own city. Jesus grows up there and returns to it after the Passover visit at age twelve, being subject to his parents.

l: Bethlehem, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: Bethlehem is David's city, where Joseph must enroll because he is of David's house. Jesus is born there, and the shepherds come there to find the baby in the feeding trough after the angel's announcement.

l: Jerusalem, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: Jerusalem is where Jesus is brought to be presented to the Lord and where a sacrifice is offered according to the law. Simeon and Anna meet him there in the temple. His parents go there every year for the Passover, and when he is twelve he stays behind and is found after three days in the temple among the teachers.

l: shepherds, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: Shepherds keeping watch over their flock by night in the field are terrified when an angel of the Lord appears to them. They go with haste to Bethlehem, find Mary, Joseph, and the baby in the feeding trough, and publicize widely what had been said about the child. They return glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen.

l: angel (the angel of the Lord), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: The angel of the Lord stands by the shepherds, the glory of the Lord shining around them, and tells them not to be afraid. He announces good news of great joy: a Savior, Christ the Lord, is born in David's city, and the sign is a baby wrapped in cloth lying in a feeding trough. A multitude of the heavenly army then joins him, and afterward the angels go away into the sky. It is also noted that the angel had given Jesus' name before he was conceived.

l: God, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: God is praised by the heavenly army with "Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good will toward men," and glorified by the shepherds and by Simeon. His law, called the law of the Lord and of Moses, governs the circumcision, purification, presentation, and sacrifice. The grace of God is upon the child Jesus, who increases in favor with God and men, and Jesus refers to the temple as his Father's house.

l: Simeon, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: Simeon is a righteous and devout man in Jerusalem, looking for the consolation of Israel, with the Holy Spirit on him. It had been revealed to him that he would not see death before seeing the Lord's Christ. He comes into the temple in the Spirit, takes Jesus in his arms, blesses God, says his eyes have seen God's salvation, and tells Mary the child is appointed for the falling and rising of many in Israel and that a sword will pierce her soul.

l: Anna, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: Anna is a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel of the tribe of Asher, of great age, who lived with a husband seven years and had been a widow for about eighty-four years. She never departs from the temple, worshiping with fastings and petitions night and day. Coming up at the very hour of Simeon's blessing, she gives thanks to the Lord and speaks of Jesus to all who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem.

l: enrollment (census), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: A decree from Caesar Augustus calls for all the world to be enrolled, the first enrollment made when Quirinius was governor of Syria. Everyone goes to his own city to enroll. This brings Joseph and Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born.

l: birth of Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: While Joseph and Mary are in Bethlehem for the enrollment, the day comes for Mary to give birth to her firstborn son. She wraps him in bands of cloth and lays him in a feeding trough because there was no room in the inn. An angel announces the birth to shepherds as the birth of a Savior, Christ the Lord, and the shepherds find the child as told.

l: presentation of Jesus at the temple, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 2
s: When the days of purification according to the law of Moses are fulfilled, Joseph and Mary bring Jesus up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as the law says every male who opens the womb shall be called holy, and to offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. Simeon takes the child in his arms, blesses God, and speaks of him as salvation and a light for the nations, and Anna gives thanks and speaks of him. The parents then return to Nazareth after accomplishing everything the law required.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 3
s: In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the word of God comes to John, son of Zacharias, in the wilderness, and he preaches a baptism of repentance around the Jordan, in fulfillment of Isaiah's words. John warns the multitudes to produce fruits worthy of repentance and gives practical instructions to crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers. He tells the people that one mightier than he will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, and Herod the tetrarch, reproved by John, shuts him up in prison. Jesus is baptized and, while praying, sees the Holy Spirit descend like a dove as a voice from the sky calls him beloved Son. The chapter closes with a genealogy of Jesus, about thirty years old, tracing back through David, Abraham, and Noah to Adam, the son of God.

l: John, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 3
s: John, son of Zacharias, receives the word of God in the wilderness and preaches a baptism of repentance for remission of sins around the Jordan. He rebukes the multitudes, instructs crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers, and says one mightier than he will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. After reproving Herod for Herodias and his other evil deeds, he is shut up in prison.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 3
s: Jesus is baptized with the people and, while he prays, the Holy Spirit descends on him like a dove and a voice from the sky calls him beloved Son, in whom God is well pleased. He is about thirty years old when he begins to teach, is supposed to be the son of Joseph, and is traced through a genealogy back to Adam, the son of God.

l: Herod the tetrarch, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 3
s: Herod is named as tetrarch of Galilee. John reproves him for taking Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all his evil deeds, and he adds to these by shutting John up in prison.

l: God, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 3
s: The word of God comes to John in the wilderness, and John says all flesh will see God's salvation and that God can raise up children to Abraham from stones. A voice from the sky declares Jesus his beloved Son, and the genealogy ends by calling Adam the son of God.

l: baptism of repentance, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 3
s: John preaches it for remission of sins throughout the region around the Jordan. Those who undergo it are told to produce fruits worthy of repentance, and John contrasts it with the coming one's baptism in the Holy Spirit and fire; Jesus is also baptized among the people.

l: multitudes (who came to John), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 3
s: The multitudes go out to be baptized by John, who calls them offspring of vipers and warns them to produce good fruit and not rely on having Abraham as father. They ask what they must do and are told to share coats and food. The people are in expectation and wonder whether John is the Christ.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 4
s: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, is led into the wilderness, where he fasts forty days and resists the devil's three temptations by quoting Scripture. He returns to Galilee and teaches in synagogues, then reads Isaiah's prophecy in the synagogue at Nazareth and says it is fulfilled in their hearing. The Nazareth crowd, angered by his words about Elijah and Elisha and the rejection of prophets in their hometown, tries to throw him off a cliff, but he passes through them and leaves. At Capernaum he teaches with authority, casts out an unclean spirit from a man in the synagogue, heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others, and silences demons who name him the Christ. When crowds try to keep him, he says he must preach God's Kingdom in other cities as well.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 4
s: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, is led into the wilderness, fasts forty days, and answers each of the devil's temptations with Scripture. In Nazareth he reads Isaiah, declares it fulfilled, and escapes a crowd that tries to throw him off a cliff. In Capernaum he teaches with authority, casts out an unclean spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others, forbids demons to speak, and says he was sent to preach God's Kingdom to other cities too.

l: Satan, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 4
s: The devil tempts Jesus for forty days, telling him to turn a stone into bread, offering him all the kingdoms of the world if he will worship him, and urging him to throw himself from the temple pinnacle while quoting Scripture. He claims the authority over the kingdoms has been delivered to him. After Jesus rebuffs each temptation, he departs until another time.

l: Nazareth, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 4
s: Nazareth is the town where Jesus was brought up and where he reads from Isaiah in the synagogue on the Sabbath. Its people doubt him as Joseph's son, grow wrathful at his words, and lead him to the brow of the hill on which the city is built to throw him off. He passes through them and goes his way.

l: Capernaum, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 4
s: Capernaum is a city of Galilee to which Jesus comes down after leaving Nazareth. He teaches there on the Sabbath, and people are astonished at his authority. It is mentioned earlier as a place where deeds attributed to him were heard of, and there he casts out a demon and heals Simon's mother-in-law.

l: temptation of Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 4
s: During forty days in the wilderness the devil tempts Jesus, who has eaten nothing and is hungry. The three temptations are to make a stone into bread, to gain all the kingdoms by worshiping the devil, and to cast himself from the temple pinnacle. Jesus answers each with Scripture, and the devil leaves until another time.

l: synagogue (Nazareth), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 4
s: In the Nazareth synagogue, Jesus stands on the Sabbath, as was his custom, and reads from the book of Isaiah. He declares the Scripture fulfilled in their hearing. His words there provoke wrath, and the people throw him out of the city.

l: synagogue crowd at Nazareth, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 4
s: The crowd in the Nazareth synagogue fastens its eyes on Jesus and wonders at his gracious words, asking whether he is Joseph's son. After he cites a proverb and the examples of Elijah and Elisha, they are filled with wrath. They throw him out of the city and try to throw him off a cliff, but he passes through them.

l: unclean spirit man, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 4
s: In the Capernaum synagogue a man with the spirit of an unclean demon cries out, calling Jesus of Nazareth the Holy One of God and asking whether he has come to destroy them. Jesus rebukes the spirit, which throws the man down in the middle of the people and comes out without harming him.

l: demons, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 4
s: Demons come out of many people, crying out that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. Jesus rebukes them and does not allow them to speak, because they knew he was the Christ. The onlookers marvel that he commands unclean spirits with authority and power and they obey.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: In Chapter 5, Jesus teaches the crowd from Simon's boat by the lake of Gennesaret and directs Simon to let down his nets, producing a huge catch; Simon, James, and John then leave everything to follow him. Jesus cleanses a man full of leprosy, then heals a paralyzed man lowered through a roof, declaring his sins forgiven, which prompts the scribes and Pharisees to accuse him of blasphemy. He calls the tax collector Levi, who leaves everything and hosts a feast, where the Pharisees and their scribes complain that Jesus eats with sinners. Asked why his disciples do not fast, Jesus answers with the image of the bridegroom and the parables of the garment and wineskins.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: Jesus teaches the crowd from Simon's boat, directs the great catch of fish, and tells Simon he will be catching people alive. He cleanses a man full of leprosy, forgives and heals a paralyzed man, calls Levi, and defends eating with sinners and his disciples' not fasting, saying he has come to call sinners to repentance.

l: Peter, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: Simon lends his boat to Jesus and, though he had caught nothing all night, lets down the net at Jesus' word. Seeing the catch he falls at Jesus' knees, calling himself a sinful man, is told he will be catching people alive, and leaves everything to follow Jesus.

l: catch of fish, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: After Jesus tells Simon to put out into the deep, the nets take a great multitude of fish, so that the net begins to break. Partners in the other boat help, and both boats fill and begin to sink, amazing Simon, James, John, and the others.

l: man full of leprosy, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: A man full of leprosy falls on his face before Jesus and says that if Jesus wants to, he can make him clean. Jesus touches him and says "I want to. Be made clean," and the leprosy leaves him immediately. Jesus commands him to tell no one but to show himself to the priest and offer for his cleansing.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: Pharisees and teachers of the law sit by as Jesus teaches, having come from every village of Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem. They and the scribes reason that Jesus blasphemes in forgiving sins, and later murmur against his disciples for eating with tax collectors and sinners and ask why Jesus' disciples do not fast.

l: paralyzed man, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: Men bring a paralyzed man on a cot and, unable to get through the crowd, lower him through the tiles before Jesus. Jesus tells him his sins are forgiven, then tells him to arise, take up his cot, and go home. He rises immediately and departs glorifying God.

l: forgiveness of sins, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: Jesus declares the paralyzed man's sins forgiven, and the scribes and Pharisees object that only God can forgive sins. Jesus heals the man so they may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.

l: Levi, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: Levi is a tax collector sitting at the tax office when Jesus says "Follow me!" He leaves everything, rises, and follows Jesus, and makes a great feast for him in his house.

l: feast at Levi's house, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: Levi hosts a great feast for Jesus at his house, attended by a great crowd of tax collectors and others. The scribes and Pharisees murmur against the disciples for eating and drinking with sinners, and Jesus answers that the sick need a physician and that he came to call sinners to repentance.

l: fasting, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: Jesus is asked why John's disciples and the Pharisees' disciples often fast and pray while his disciples eat and drink. He answers that the friends of the bridegroom cannot be made to fast while the bridegroom is with them, but that when he is taken away, they will fast in those days.

l: parable of garments and wineskins, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 5
s: Jesus tells that no one puts a piece of a new garment on an old one, and no one puts new wine into old wineskins, since the new would tear the old garment and burst the skins. New wine must go into fresh wineskins, and he adds that no one who has drunk old wine immediately desires new, saying 'The old is better.'

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: Chapter 6 opens with Jesus' disciples plucking grain on the Sabbath, which draws a challenge from some Pharisees; Jesus answers by citing David and declares the Son of Man lord of the Sabbath. On another Sabbath he heals a man's withered right hand in the synagogue while the scribes and Pharisees watch for an accusation, and they are filled with rage. After a night of prayer on the mountain, Jesus chooses twelve apostles from his disciples and names them, then comes down to a level place where a great crowd gathers to hear him and be healed. There he teaches his disciples with blessings and woes, commands love for enemies, mercy, giving, and not judging, and warns about blind guides, specks and beams, and trees known by their fruit. He closes by asking why people call him 'Lord, Lord' without doing what he says, and contrasts the man who builds on rock with the one who builds without a foundation.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: Jesus defends his disciples against the Pharisees by citing David and declares the Son of Man lord of the Sabbath, then heals a man's withered hand on a Sabbath after asking whether it is lawful to do good or harm. He prays all night, chooses twelve apostles, heals the crowd as power comes out of him, and teaches blessings, woes, love of enemies, mercy, and obedience to his words.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: The disciples pluck and eat grain on the Sabbath and are questioned by some Pharisees. Jesus later chooses twelve of them as apostles and addresses to them the blessings, woes, and teaching on love, mercy, not judging, and doing his words.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: Some Pharisees challenge the disciples for plucking grain on the Sabbath. Together with the scribes they watch Jesus to see whether he will heal on the Sabbath so they can accuse him, and after he heals the withered hand they are filled with rage and discuss what to do to him.

l: Sabbath, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: The Sabbath is the setting of two conflicts: the plucking of grain and the healing of the withered hand. Jesus declares the Son of Man lord of the Sabbath and asks whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or harm, to save a life or kill.

l: God, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: God's house is where David entered and ate the show bread, which only the priests may lawfully eat. Jesus prays to God all night, says God's Kingdom belongs to the poor, and calls him the Most High who is kind to the unthankful and evil and merciful as a Father.

l: man with the withered hand, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: A man with a withered right hand is in the synagogue on a Sabbath. Jesus, knowing the thoughts of those watching, has him stand in the middle and tells him to stretch out his hand, and it is restored as sound as the other.

l: the twelve, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: After praying all night, Jesus chooses twelve from his disciples and names them apostles: Simon (named Peter), Andrew, James, John, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.

l: multitude, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: A great number of people from all Judea, Jerusalem, and the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon gather on the level place to hear Jesus and be healed of diseases and unclean spirits. All the multitude seek to touch him because power comes out of him and heals them all.

l: Beatitudes and woes, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: Jesus blesses the poor, the hungry, the weeping, and those hated for the Son of Man's sake, promising God's Kingdom, fullness, laughter, and great reward in heaven. He pronounces woes on the rich, the full, those who laugh now, and those of whom men speak well, warning of hunger, mourning, and the pattern of the fathers with the false prophets.

l: enemies, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: Jesus commands his hearers to love their enemies, do good to those who hate them, bless those who curse them, and pray for those who mistreat them. He says doing so, and lending expecting nothing back, brings great reward and makes them children of the Most High.

l: love and mercy, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: Jesus teaches the golden-rule standard of doing to others as one would like done to oneself and says loving only those who love you earns no credit, since sinners do the same. He urges being merciful as the Father is merciful, not judging or condemning, setting free, and giving generously, with the same measure returned.

l: wise and foolish builders, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 6
s: Jesus asks why people call him 'Lord, Lord' and do not do what he says. He likens the one who hears and does his words to a man who builds on rock, whose house withstands the flood, and the one who hears and does not do to a man who builds without a foundation, whose house falls in great ruin.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 7
s: In Capernaum, Jesus heals a centurion's dying servant from a distance after the centurion, who sent Jewish elders and friends to speak for him, shows faith in Jesus' word, and Jesus praises that faith. At Nain, Jesus raises a widow's only son from his coffin, and the crowd glorifies God and spreads the report throughout Judea. John the Baptizer sends two disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one who is coming, and Jesus points to his works and then tells the crowds that John is a prophet and more than a prophet, while criticizing the generation that rejects both John and himself. At the house of a Pharisee named Simon, a sinful woman weeps on Jesus' feet and anoints them, and Jesus uses a parable of two debtors to rebuke Simon, declare the woman's sins forgiven, and send her away in peace because of her faith.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 7
s: Jesus heals the centurion's servant without entering the house and marvels at the centurion's faith. He raises the widow's son at Nain, answers John's disciples by pointing to his works, and speaks to the crowds about John. At Simon's house he tells the parable of the two debtors, forgives the sinful woman's sins, and tells her that her faith has saved her.

l: centurion, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 7
s: The centurion, whose servant was dear to him, sent Jewish elders and then friends to ask Jesus to heal the servant, saying he was not worthy to have Jesus come under his roof. He explained that, as a man under authority, he knew Jesus need only say the word, and Jesus said he had not found such great faith, not even in Israel. The elders said he loved the nation and had built their synagogue.

l: servant (the centurion's servant), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 7
s: The centurion's servant was sick and at the point of death. When the men sent by the centurion returned to the house, they found that the servant was well.

l: widow of Nain, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 7
s: The widow of Nain was following the coffin of her only son out of the city gate, with many townspeople with her, when Jesus saw her and had compassion, telling her not to cry. Jesus then raised her son and gave him back to her.

l: young man (the widow's son), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 7
s: The widow's only son was dead and being carried out of Nain in a coffin. Jesus touched the coffin and told him to arise, and he sat up and began to speak, after which Jesus gave him to his mother.

l: John, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 7
s: John heard about Jesus' works from his disciples and sent two of them to ask whether Jesus was the one who is coming or whether they should look for another. Jesus later tells the crowds that John is a prophet and much more, the messenger foretold in writing, and that none born of women is a greater prophet, though the least in God's Kingdom is greater. Jesus also notes that people said John had a demon because he came neither eating bread nor drinking wine.

l: disciples of John, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 7
s: John's disciples told him about Jesus' works, and two of them were sent to Jesus with John's question about whether he was the coming one. Jesus told them to report to John what they had seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news preached to them.

l: Simon the Pharisee, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 7
s: Simon, a Pharisee, invited Jesus to eat at his house and thought to himself that Jesus could not be a prophet or he would know the woman touching him was a sinner. Jesus told him the parable of the two debtors, and Simon answered that the one forgiven more would love more. Jesus then contrasted Simon's lack of water, kiss, and oil with the woman's actions.

l: sinful woman, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 7
s: A woman known in the city as a sinner came to Simon's house with an alabaster jar of ointment, wept at Jesus' feet, wiped them with her hair, kissed them, and anointed them. Jesus said her many sins were forgiven because she loved much, and he told her that her faith had saved her and to go in peace.

l: forgiveness of sins, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 7
s: Jesus teaches through the parable of the two debtors that the one forgiven more loves more, and applies it to the woman, saying her many sins are forgiven because she loved much while one forgiven little loves little. He tells her directly that her sins are forgiven, and those at the table ask among themselves who this is who even forgives sins.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 8
s: Jesus travels through cities and villages preaching God's Kingdom, accompanied by the twelve and several women, including Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna, who support them. He teaches the parable of the sower to a large crowd and explains it privately to his disciples, then speaks of the lamp and of hearing carefully. He calms a storm on the lake, heals a man possessed by a legion of demons in the country of the Gadarenes, and sends the man home to declare what God did for him. Back across the lake, Jairus asks him to heal his dying twelve-year-old daughter; on the way a woman with a twelve-year-old flow of blood touches his cloak and is healed, and Jesus then raises Jairus' daughter, telling her parents to tell no one.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 8
s: Jesus preaches through cities and villages, teaches the parable of the sower and explains it to his disciples, and says his true mother and brothers are those who hear and do God's word. He rebukes the wind and water, casts the legion of demons from a man into pigs, heals the woman with the flow of blood, and raises Jairus' daughter by taking her hand and saying 'Child, arise!'

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 8
s: The twelve accompany Jesus, and they ask him what the parable of the sower means; he tells them they are given to know the mysteries of God's Kingdom. In the boat they wake him in fear of dying in the storm, are asked 'Where is your faith?', and marvel at his command over wind and water. Peter speaks up when Jesus asks who touched him, and Peter, John and James are the only disciples allowed into Jairus' house.

l: parable of the sower, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 8
s: Jesus tells of a farmer whose seed falls along the road, on rock, among thorns, and on good ground, where it yields a hundredfold. He explains that the seed is the word of God and the soils are different hearers: those from whom the devil takes the word, those who fall away in temptation, those choked by cares, riches and pleasures, and those who hold it tightly and bear fruit with perseverance.

l: storm (wind and water), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 8
s: A wind storm comes down on the lake while Jesus sleeps in the boat, and the boat takes on dangerous amounts of water. Jesus rebukes the wind and the raging water, and they cease and it becomes calm, leaving the disciples asking who he is that even winds and water obey him.

l: possessed man (Legion), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 8
s: A man from the city of the Gadarenes, long possessed by demons, wore no clothes and lived in the tombs, and had broken chains and fetters. He falls before Jesus, names himself Legion, and is freed when the demons leave; people then find him sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind. He begs to go with Jesus but is sent home to declare what God has done, and he proclaims throughout the city what Jesus did for him.

l: demons, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 8
s: The many demons in the man call Jesus Son of the Most High God and beg not to be sent into the abyss. Jesus allows them to enter a herd of pigs, which rush down the steep bank into the lake and drown.

l: Jairus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 8
s: Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, falls at Jesus' feet and begs him to come to his house because his only daughter, about twelve, is dying. When word comes that she is dead, Jesus tells him not to be afraid and only believe, and Jairus and his wife see their daughter raised and are told to tell no one.

l: Jairus' daughter, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 8
s: Jairus' only daughter, about twelve years old, is dying and then dies before Jesus arrives. Jesus says she is sleeping, takes her by the hand and calls 'Child, arise!'; her spirit returns, she rises immediately, and he orders that she be given something to eat.

l: woman with flow of blood, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 8
s: A woman who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years and spent all she had on physicians without being healed touches the fringe of Jesus' cloak from behind, and the bleeding stops immediately. When Jesus asks who touched him, she comes trembling and declares before everyone why she touched him; he calls her 'Daughter,' says her faith has made her well, and tells her to go in peace.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: In Luke 9, Jesus gives the twelve power over demons and disease and sends them out to preach and heal, while Herod wonders who Jesus is. After the apostles return, Jesus withdraws toward Bethsaida, teaches and heals the multitudes who follow, and feeds about five thousand men with five loaves and two fish. Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ of God, and Jesus foretells his suffering, death and resurrection and calls those who would follow him to deny themselves and take up their cross. On the mountain with Peter, John and James, Jesus is transfigured, Moses and Elijah appear, and a voice from a cloud calls him God's beloved Son. Jesus then heals a boy the disciples could not help, corrects the disciples' arguments about greatness, their rebuke of an outside exorcist, and James and John's wish to call down fire on a Samaritan village, and he sets his face toward Jerusalem while answering three would-be followers.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: Jesus sends out the twelve, feeds the multitude, is confessed by Peter as the Christ of God, and is transfigured before Peter, John and James. He twice foretells that he will be delivered up and killed, heals the possessed boy, and sets his face toward Jerusalem, teaching about the cost of following him.

l: the twelve, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: The twelve are given power and authority over demons and disease and are sent to preach and heal, going through the villages. They urge Jesus to send the crowd away, distribute the bread and fish, fail to cast out the boy's spirit, do not understand his saying about being delivered up, and argue about who is greatest.

l: Peter, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: Peter answers Jesus's question with the confession that he is "The Christ of God." On the mountain he proposes making three tents for Jesus, Moses and Elijah, "not knowing what he said."

l: God, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: God is the source of the Kingdom the twelve preach, and the multitude is astonished at his majesty after the boy is healed. A voice from the cloud declares, "This is my beloved Son. Listen to him!" Jesus says that whoever receives him receives the one who sent him.

l: God's Kingdom, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: God's Kingdom is what the twelve are sent to preach and what Jesus speaks of to the multitudes. Jesus says some standing there will not taste death until they see it, and that one who looks back after putting his hand to the plow is not fit for it.

l: multitude (at Bethsaida), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: The multitudes follow Jesus when he withdraws toward Bethsaida, and he welcomes them, speaks to them of God's Kingdom and cures those needing healing. About five thousand men are seated in groups of about fifty and all eat and are filled.

l: feeding of the five thousand, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: As the day wears on, Jesus tells the twelve to give the crowd something to eat, though they have only five loaves and two fish. He blesses and breaks them, the disciples set them before the multitude, all eat and are filled, and twelve baskets of pieces are left over.

l: transfiguration, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: About eight days after his sayings, Jesus goes up the mountain with Peter, John and James to pray, and his face changes and his clothing becomes white and dazzling. Moses and Elijah appear in glory and speak of his departure at Jerusalem, a cloud overshadows them, and a voice names him the beloved Son. Afterwards the three tell no one what they saw.

l: boy (the man's son), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: The boy is the only child of a man in the crowd and is seized by a spirit that makes him cry out, convulse and foam, and bruises him. The disciples could not cast it out, but Jesus rebukes the unclean spirit, heals him and gives him back to his father.

l: Jesus's suffering, death and resurrection, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: Jesus says the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and be raised the third day. He later says he will be delivered into the hands of men, but the disciples do not understand and are afraid to ask. Moses and Elijah also speak of his departure to be accomplished at Jerusalem.

l: discipleship, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 9
s: Jesus teaches that anyone who would follow him must deny himself, take up his cross, and lose his life for his sake in order to save it. He teaches that the least is the greatest, tells the disciples not to forbid one who is not against them, and answers three would-be followers, telling them that following him means no place to lay one's head, no delay for burying a father, and no looking back.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 10
s: Jesus appoints seventy others and sends them two by two ahead of him into cities, instructing them to travel without provisions, offer peace to houses, heal the sick, and proclaim that God's Kingdom has come near, while pronouncing woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum. The seventy return rejoicing that demons are subject to them, and Jesus tells them to rejoice instead that their names are written in heaven. Jesus thanks his Father for revealing these things to little children and says that only the Son reveals the Father. When a lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, Jesus draws out the command to love God and neighbor and tells the parable of a man attacked by robbers, who is ignored by a priest and a Levite but cared for by a Samaritan. Finally, Martha receives Jesus into her house, complains that her sister Mary sits at his feet instead of helping, and Jesus says Mary has chosen the good part.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 10
s: Jesus appoints and sends out the seventy with instructions, pronounces woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum, and says he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. He rejoices in the Holy Spirit, thanks the Father, and declares that all things have been delivered to him. He answers a lawyer with the parable of the Samaritan, and tells Martha that Mary has chosen the good part.

l: seventy others, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 10
s: The seventy are appointed and sent two by two ahead of Jesus, as lambs among wolves, to heal the sick and announce that God's Kingdom has come near. They return with joy that even demons are subject to them in Jesus' name, and Jesus gives them authority over serpents, scorpions, and the enemy's power, urging them to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.

l: God, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 10
s: The Father is addressed by Jesus as Lord of heaven and earth, who has hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children, as was well-pleasing in his sight. Jesus says the Father has delivered all things to him, that only the Son knows the Father, and that the Son reveals him to whomever he desires.

l: God's Kingdom, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 10
s: The seventy are told to announce that God's Kingdom has come near to the cities they enter, whether those cities receive them or reject them. Rejecting the messengers brings a warning of a worse judgment than that of Sodom.

l: lawyer, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 10
s: A lawyer stands up to test Jesus by asking what he must do to inherit eternal life. He correctly answers with the command to love God and neighbor, then, desiring to justify himself, asks who his neighbor is. After Jesus' parable he answers that the one who showed mercy was the neighbor, and is told to go and do likewise.

l: man attacked by robbers, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 10
s: In Jesus' parable, a man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho is stripped, beaten, and left half dead by robbers. A priest and a Levite pass by on the other side, but a Samaritan bandages his wounds, takes him to an inn, and pays for his care.

l: Samaritan, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 10
s: In the parable, the Samaritan is moved with compassion on seeing the wounded man, bandages his wounds with oil and wine, and carries him on his own animal to an inn. He pays two denarii to the host and promises to repay any further expense, and is identified as the one who showed mercy and was a neighbor.

l: Martha, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 10
s: Martha receives Jesus into her house in a village. Distracted with much serving, she asks Jesus to tell her sister to help her, and Jesus replies that she is anxious and troubled about many things when only one thing is needed.

l: Mary, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 10
s: Mary is Martha's sister and sits at Jesus' feet hearing his word while Martha serves. Jesus says she has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: In Luke 11, Jesus, asked by a disciple to teach them to pray, gives a model prayer and the parable of the friend at midnight, urging persistent asking, seeking, and knocking, and assures them the heavenly Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. After he casts out a mute demon, some accuse him of acting by Beelzebul while others demand a sign, and he answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand and that by God's finger the Kingdom of God has come. He calls his generation evil, promises only the sign of Jonah, and says the Queen of the South and the men of Nineveh will condemn it. At a Pharisee's dinner he pronounces a series of woes on the Pharisees and lawyers for hypocrisy, burdening others, killing prophets, and taking away the key of knowledge. The scribes and Pharisees become terribly angry and lie in wait to catch him in his words.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: Jesus teaches his disciples to pray after they ask, tells the parable of the friend at midnight, and casts out a mute demon.
