He answers accusations of working by Beelzebul, calls his generation evil, and pronounces woes on the Pharisees and lawyers at a Pharisee's table, after which the scribes and Pharisees lie in wait to accuse him.

l: God, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: God is addressed as 'Our Father in heaven' in the prayer and described as a heavenly Father who gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. His finger is the power by which Jesus casts out demons, and his wisdom speaks of sending prophets and apostles whose blood will be required of this generation.

l: God's Kingdom, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: The prayer asks that God's Kingdom come. Jesus says that if he casts out demons by God's finger, then God's Kingdom has come to his hearers, and he contrasts it with Satan's kingdom, which cannot stand if divided.

l: prayer, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: A disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray as John taught his disciples, and Jesus gives a prayer addressed to the Father asking for his name to be kept holy, his Kingdom to come, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from the evil one. He urges persistence in asking, seeking, and knocking, promising that everyone who asks receives.

l: friend at midnight (parable), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: Jesus tells of a man who goes to a friend at midnight to borrow three loaves for a visitor, and the friend inside refuses because the door is shut and his children are in bed. Jesus says that because of the man's persistence the friend will get up and give him as many as he needs.

l: demon (cast out by Jesus), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: Jesus casts out a demon that made a man mute, and the man speaks, causing the crowds to marvel. The act prompts both the accusation of collusion with Beelzebul and the demand for a sign.

l: Satan, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: Some in the crowd claim Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons. Jesus replies that a divided kingdom falls, asks by whom their own children cast out demons, and says he acts by God's finger.

l: this generation, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: Jesus calls this generation evil because it seeks a sign, and says it will receive only the sign of Jonah. He says the Queen of the South and the men of Nineveh will condemn it in the judgment, and that the blood of all the prophets will be required of it.

l: Jonah, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: Jonah is named as the sign given to this generation: as he was a sign to the Ninevites, the Son of Man will be to this generation. Jesus says the men of Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching and that one greater than Jonah is present.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: Some of the crowd and a Pharisee host react to Jesus, and the Pharisee marvels that Jesus did not wash before dinner. Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for cleaning the outside of the cup while being full of extortion and wickedness, for tithing herbs while bypassing justice and love, and for loving the best seats. The scribes and Pharisees then grow angry and lie in wait to catch him in his words.

l: lawyers, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: A lawyer objects that Jesus' rebuke insults them too. Jesus pronounces woes on them for loading people with burdens they will not lift a finger to help carry, building the tombs of prophets their fathers killed, and taking away the key of knowledge.

l: woes against Pharisees and lawyers, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 11
s: Jesus pronounces three woes on the Pharisees, for tithing herbs but neglecting justice and love, loving the best seats and greetings, and being like hidden graves. He pronounces three on the lawyers, for burdening people, building tombs of prophets their fathers killed, and taking away the key of knowledge. The woes provoke the anger of the scribes and Pharisees.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: In Chapter 12, with a vast multitude gathered, Jesus first warns his disciples against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and tells them to fear God rather than those who kill the body, assuring them of God's care and of the Holy Spirit's help when they are brought before authorities. When a man in the crowd asks him to settle an inheritance, Jesus warns against covetousness and tells the parable of a rich man who stores up goods and loses his life that night. He then tells his disciples not to be anxious about food or clothing, pointing to ravens and lilies, and urges them to seek God's Kingdom, give to the needy, and be watchful like servants awaiting their lord. In answer to Peter, he describes the faithful and wise steward and the greater accountability of those given much, then speaks of bringing fire and division even within households. Finally he rebukes the multitudes as hypocrites for not interpreting the time and urges settling with an adversary before reaching the judge.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: Jesus warns his disciples about hypocrisy, fear, and anxiety, refuses to act as judge over an inheritance dispute, and teaches through a parable of a rich man, images of ravens and lilies, and sayings about watchful servants. He declares that he came to throw fire on the earth, that he has a baptism to undergo and is distressed until it is accomplished, and that he has come to bring division rather than peace. He rebukes the multitudes as hypocrites for failing to interpret the present time.

l: disciples, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: The disciples are addressed first, warned against the yeast of the Pharisees, told not to fear those who kill the body, and promised the Holy Spirit will teach them what to say before authorities. They are told not to be anxious about food or clothing, to seek God's Kingdom, to sell and give to the needy, and to be ready for the Son of Man's coming. Peter asks on their behalf whether the parable is for them or for everybody.

l: multitude, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: A multitude of many thousands gathers, so crowded that they trample on each other. One man from it asks Jesus to tell his brother to divide an inheritance with him and is answered with a warning against covetousness. Later Jesus calls the multitudes hypocrites for being able to read the earth and sky but not interpreting this time.

l: God, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: God is presented as the one to fear, who after killing has power to cast into Gehenna, and as one who does not forget even one sparrow. He feeds the ravens, clothes the grass, and knows his people's needs as Father, giving them the Kingdom as his good pleasure. In the parable he tells the rich man that his soul is required that night.

l: rich man (in the parable), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: The rich man's ground produces abundantly, and he plans to pull down his barns and build bigger ones to store his grain and goods, then to take his ease, eat, drink, and be merry. God calls him a foolish one and says his soul is required that night, asking whose his prepared things will be. He illustrates one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.

l: covetousness, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: Jesus tells the crowd to beware of and keep themselves from covetousness, because a man's life does not consist of the abundance of his possessions. The parable of the rich man who stores up goods illustrates its folly. It is contrasted with selling possessions, giving to the needy, and storing treasure in the heavens.

l: anxiety about necessities, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: Jesus tells his disciples not to be anxious about what they will eat or wear, since life is more than food and the body more than clothing. He notes that being anxious cannot add a cubit to one's height, and points to ravens and lilies as examples of God's provision. He says the nations seek these things but the Father knows the disciples need them, and that seeking God's Kingdom will bring them.

l: God's Kingdom, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: Jesus tells his disciples to seek God's Kingdom, promising that all these necessities will be added to them. He says it is the Father's good pleasure to give the Kingdom to the little flock, who should therefore not be afraid.

l: watchful servants, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: Jesus tells his hearers to have their waists dressed and lamps burning, like men watching for their lord's return from a wedding feast. Those servants found watching are blessed, and the lord will dress himself, make them recline, and serve them, even if he comes in the second or third watch. The image is tied to being ready for the Son of Man, who comes in an unexpected hour.

l: faithful steward, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: In answer to Peter, Jesus describes the faithful and wise steward set over his lord's household to give portions of food at the right times. If found doing so when the lord comes, he will be blessed and set over all the lord has. A servant who instead says the lord delays, beats the other servants, and gets drunk will be cut in two and placed with the unfaithful, and those given much will have much required.

l: division in households, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 12
s: Jesus says he has come to bring division on the earth rather than peace. He states that five in one house will be divided, three against two and two against three. He lists father against son, mother against daughter, and mother-in-law against daughter-in-law, with each pair also opposed in reverse.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 13
s: Jesus responds to news of Galileans killed by Pilate and to those killed by a falling tower in Siloam by calling his hearers to repent or perish, and he tells a parable of a fig tree that bore no fruit and was given one more year. On a Sabbath in a synagogue he frees a woman bent over for eighteen years, and the ruler of the synagogue objects; Jesus rebukes him and the crowd rejoices. He compares God's Kingdom to a mustard seed and to yeast, then, while traveling toward Jerusalem, answers a question about how many are saved by urging people to strive to enter the narrow door. Pharisees warn him that Herod wants to kill him; he replies that he must continue his work and that a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem, and he laments over Jerusalem, which he says is left desolate.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 13
s: Jesus tells his hearers that those killed by Pilate and by the tower were not worse sinners and that all must repent or perish. He heals a bent woman on the Sabbath, rebukes the ruler of the synagogue, teaches parables of the mustard seed and yeast, and urges people to strive for the narrow door. Traveling toward Jerusalem, he answers the Pharisees' warning about Herod by calling him a fox, says he must continue his work, and laments over Jerusalem.

l: Jerusalem, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 13
s: Jesus is traveling on toward Jerusalem and says a prophet cannot perish outside it. He addresses it as the city that kills the prophets and stones those sent to it, says he wanted to gather its children like a hen gathers her brood but they refused, and declares its house left desolate. He says they will not see him until they say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!'

l: fig tree parable, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 13
s: A man whose fig tree in his vineyard has produced no fruit for three years tells the vine dresser to cut it down for wasting the soil. The vine dresser asks to leave it one more year while he digs around it and fertilizes it. If it bears fruit it stays; if not, it may be cut down.

l: woman with a spirit of infirmity, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 13
s: She had been bent over for eighteen years and could not straighten up. Jesus called her, told her she was freed from her infirmity, and laid his hands on her, and she immediately stood straight and glorified God. Jesus calls her a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound.

l: ruler of the synagogue, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 13
s: The ruler of the synagogue, indignant that Jesus healed on the Sabbath, told the crowd to come for healing on the six working days and not on the Sabbath. Jesus answered him, calling him and those with him hypocrites, and pointed out that each of them frees an ox or donkey on the Sabbath. Jesus's adversaries were disappointed afterward.

l: Sabbath, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 13
s: Jesus heals the bent woman in a synagogue on the Sabbath, and the ruler of the synagogue objects that healing belongs on the six working days. Jesus replies that people untie their ox or donkey to water it on the Sabbath, so the woman ought to be freed from her bondage on that day.

l: God's Kingdom, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 13
s: Jesus compares it to a mustard seed that grows into a large tree in which birds live, and to yeast a woman hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened. He says people will come from east, west, north and south to sit down in it, and that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the prophets are in it. Some who are excluded will weep, and the last will be first and the first last.

l: narrow door, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 13
s: In answer to whether few are saved, Jesus urges people to strive to enter by the narrow door, saying many will seek to enter and not be able. Once the master of the house has shut the door, those outside who knock and claim to have eaten and drunk in his presence will be told he does not know them and to depart, workers of iniquity.

l: repentance, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 13
s: Jesus twice says that unless his hearers repent they will all perish in the same way, after mentioning the Galileans killed by Pilate and the eighteen killed by the falling tower in Siloam. He denies that those victims were worse sinners or offenders than others. The fig tree parable, with its extra year to bear fruit, follows.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: Jesus goes to eat at the house of one of the rulers of the Pharisees on a Sabbath, where he is watched. He heals a man with dropsy after asking the lawyers and Pharisees whether healing on the Sabbath is lawful, and they stay silent and cannot answer his question about rescuing a son or an ox. He teaches the invited guests to take the lowest place and tells his host to invite the poor, maimed, lame, and blind rather than those who can repay. In response to a guest's remark about feasting in God's Kingdom, he tells of a man whose great supper is refused by invited guests with excuses, so the poor and others are brought in instead. Turning to the great multitudes, he sets out the demands of discipleship, using the images of a tower builder and a king to teach counting the cost, and ends with the saying about tasteless salt.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: Jesus, while being watched at a Pharisee ruler's house on a Sabbath, heals a man with dropsy and asks whether healing on the Sabbath is lawful. He teaches guests about the best seats and humility, tells his host to invite those who cannot repay, and speaks the parable of the great supper. He then tells the multitudes that disciples must put him above family and their own life, bear their cross, and renounce all they have.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: The lawyers and Pharisees watch Jesus and are asked whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath. They are silent and then cannot answer him about pulling a son or ox out of a well.

l: ruler of the Pharisees (host of the Sabbath meal), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: He hosts a Sabbath meal at his house where Jesus is watched. Jesus tells him not to invite friends, brothers, kinsmen, or rich neighbors who can repay him, but the poor, maimed, lame, and blind, and he will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.

l: man with dropsy, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: A man with dropsy is in front of Jesus at the meal. Jesus takes him, heals him, and lets him go.

l: Sabbath, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: The meal takes place on a Sabbath, and the people there watch Jesus. Jesus points out that any of them would immediately pull a son or ox out of a well on a Sabbath day.

l: healing on the Sabbath, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: Jesus asks the lawyers and Pharisees whether healing on the Sabbath is lawful, and they do not answer. He heals the man with dropsy anyway and justifies it by the example of rescuing a son or ox from a well.

l: best seats and lowest place, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: Jesus notices that the invited guests choose the best seats. He teaches that at a wedding feast one should take the lowest place, so the host may say 'Friend, move up higher' and the guest be honored, rather than being shamed by being told to make room for someone more honorable.

l: humility and exaltation, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: Jesus states that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. This closes his teaching about seats at the wedding feast.

l: the poor, maimed, lame, and blind, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: Jesus tells his host to invite the poor, maimed, lame, and blind to a feast, since they cannot repay and he will be blessed. In the parable, the supper host also has them brought in from the streets and lanes of the city after the invited guests refuse.

l: man who made a great supper, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: In Jesus' parable, he invites many to a great supper and becomes angry when they make excuses. He orders his servant to bring in the poor, maimed, blind, and lame, then to compel people from the highways and hedges so his house is filled, and declares none of the invited men will taste his supper.

l: servant (of the supper host), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: The servant is sent at supper time to tell the invited that everything is ready, and reports their excuses to his lord. He brings in the poor, maimed, blind, and lame, reports there is still room, and is then sent to the highways and hedges to compel others to come in.

l: great supper, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: The great supper is made by a man who invites many, and everything is ready at supper time. The invited refuse, so the house is filled with others, and the host says none of the originally invited will taste it.

l: invited guests who made excuses, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: All the invited guests, as one, begin to make excuses: one has bought a field, one has bought five yoke of oxen, and one has married a wife. The host declares that none of them will taste his supper.

l: discipleship, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: Jesus tells the multitudes that a person cannot be his disciple unless he disregards family and his own life, bears his own cross and comes after him, and renounces all he has. He ends with the saying that salt which has become tasteless is fit for neither soil nor manure pile and is thrown out.

l: counting the cost, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 14
s: Jesus illustrates it with a man who wants to build a tower and sits down first to see if he can finish, lest he be mocked. He also cites a king who weighs ten thousand against twenty thousand and sends an envoy to ask for peace terms.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: Tax collectors and sinners come near to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes murmur that he welcomes and eats with sinners. In response Jesus tells three parables: a man who leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one lost sheep, a woman who lights a lamp and sweeps to find one lost drachma coin, and a father with two sons. In the third parable the younger son takes his share of the property, wastes it, falls into famine and feeding pigs, then returns repentant, and the father runs to him, restores him, and holds a feast. The elder son is angry and refuses to go in, and the father begs him and explains that celebrating was appropriate because his brother was dead and is alive, lost and found. The first two parables conclude that there is joy in heaven and among God's angels over one sinner who repents.

l: sinners, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: The tax collectors and sinners were all coming close to Jesus to hear him. They are the ones the Pharisees and scribes complain he welcomes and eats with.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: The Pharisees and scribes murmur that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them. Jesus responds to them by telling the parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the two sons.

l: shepherd (man with one hundred sheep), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: In the parable, the man who loses one of his hundred sheep leaves the ninety-nine in the wilderness and goes after the lost one until he finds it. He carries it home on his shoulders rejoicing and calls his friends and neighbors to rejoice with him.

l: lost sheep (shepherd's sheep), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: The one sheep out of one hundred is lost and is sought until found. The shepherd carries it on his shoulders, and its finding is the occasion for rejoicing.
